summary: Describes an engineering model for adding a precision time-of-day function to an operating system kernel. The model is based on disciplined oscillators and phase-lock loops, ideas from engineering. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A clock that drifts can be nudged a tiny bit each second to stay right. This describes how a computer can keep nudging itself to match true time.

subtitle: How operating system kernels can keep accurate time using feedback loops.

tldr.problem: Computer clocks drift and lose accuracy over time, making it hard to synchronize time across a network. Traditional Unix adjustments are coarse and create jitter.
tldr.mechanism: A phase-lock loop (PLL) in the kernel continuously adjusts the clock frequency based on time corrections from the Network Time Protocol (NTP), like a servo system that learns and compensates for the oscillator's drift.
tldr.outcome: System clocks can maintain microsecond-level accuracy and stability without requiring frequent adjustments from user programs, while external precision sources like GPS can discipline the oscillator to even higher accuracy.

facts.label: Microsecond-precision reading
facts.value: Supported on Sun, Digital Ultrix, and OSF/1

today: RFC 1589 is Informational and has not been superseded. The kernel PLL model it describes influenced modern system clock implementations across Unix and Linux systems. While the specific system calls and variable names from 1994 may not be standard across all operating systems, the principles of using kernel-based PLLs with external precision sources remain foundational to high-accuracy timekeeping infrastructure.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 1589 describes a kernel model for maintaining a precise system clock in operating systems. The model uses phase-lock loops (PLL), a technique from engineering, to continuously adjust both the time and frequency of the system clock based on input from time synchronization protocols like NTP. The goal is to minimize clock errors and jitter while reducing the overhead of frequent system calls. This approach has been implemented in Unix kernels for Sun Microsystems and Digital Equipment workstations, achieving microsecond-level precision on suitable hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer keeps track of time using a quartz oscillator, but it drifts. This note explains how to nudge the clock every second based on corrections from the network so it stays accurate without jumping or jittering.

sections.title: Clock Adjustment and Frequency Discipline
sections.content:
Most Unix kernels maintain system time by counting interrupts from a hardware timer (typically 100 Hz to 1024 Hz depending on the system). The traditional adjtime() system call adjusts the clock by adding a fixed amount called tickadj at each timer interrupt for a calculated number of ticks. This has two problems: the adjustment is coarse-grained (usually about 5 microseconds), creating roundoff error, and large adjustments must be spread over many adjustment intervals, complicating the synchronization daemon.

The new kernel model replaces this with a precision-time variable that is continuously adjusted by a quantity computed from a phase-lock loop. At each timer interrupt, the kernel adds a calibrated increment that implements a type-II, first-order PLL. This allows the kernel to adjust the clock with microsecond precision and frequency control to within parts in 10^11, enabling the clock to run true even if the synchronization daemon stops or network links fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way twitches the clock in big steps, which causes jitter and rounding errors. The new way smoothly adjusts both when and how fast time advances, like a mechanical governor on an engine that learns to compensate automatically.

sections.title: Programming Interface: ntp_gettime() and ntp_adjtime()
sections.content:
The kernel model introduces two new system calls to support synchronization daemons. The ntp_gettime() call returns the current system time plus estimates of the maximum and estimated errors in microseconds, allowing applications like distributed file systems and real-time applications to know the quality of the time they are using. The ntp_adjtime() call allows the synchronization daemon to read and write kernel time-keeping variables, including the time offset, frequency offset, and PLL time constant. The daemon calls ntp_adjtime() only when a new time correction is computed (typically every 16 seconds to 1024 seconds in NTP), rather than at every second as with the old adjtime() approach. The mode parameter in ntp_adjtime() selects which variables to update via bit flags.

The kernel also maintains a clock status state machine that reflects leap-second warnings, synchronization status, and external clock health. The status can transition through states such as TIME_OK (synchronized), TIME_INS and TIME_DEL (leap-second events pending or in progress), TIME_BAD (unsynchronized), and TIME_ERR (external clock failure).
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can ask the kernel 'what time is it and how accurate is it?' and the time-keeper daemon can tell the kernel 'here is a correction and how stiff the feedback loop should be.' This replaces the old way of making many adjustments per second.

sections.title: External Precision Sources and Discipline
sections.content:
The model supports three methods for disciplining the clock to external precision sources. The first uses a pulse-per-second (PPS) signal, typically from a radio clock via a serial port modem-control lead. The kernel captures the PPS timestamp and uses it to discipline the CPU clock oscillator frequency to within a few parts in 10^8, two orders of magnitude better than an undisciplined oscillator. The second method reads time directly from an external clock interface (such as the TPRO IRIG interface) and uses the difference between the external clock and the kernel time variable to adjust the kernel PLL. The third uses a specialized precision oscillator peripheral (such as HIGHBALL) with an oven-controlled quartz oscillator that has stability of a few parts in 10^9, where the kernel PLL controls counter offsets and separately adjusts the kernel time variable.

These external precision sources allow the system clock accuracy to be limited only by the source itself and the jitter of the operating system, rather than by the poor stability of typical CPU oscillators.
sections.plainLanguage: A radio clock can send a GPS signal or a ticking pulse, and the kernel can read it directly or use it to correct the oscillator. This works like syncing a watch to the atomic clock once a second instead of every second.

sections.title: Kernel Variables and Parameters
sections.content: The kernel maintains several variables that control and reflect the state of the PLL. The time_offset variable holds the time offset in scaled microseconds (scaling factor 2^12), with a maximum range of about ±512 milliseconds and resolution of a few parts in 10^10. The time_freq variable holds the frequency offset in scaled parts-per-million (scaling factor 2^16), with a maximum range of ±256 ppm or more and resolution of parts in 10^11. The time_constant is a shift (0 to 6) that sets the PLL bandwidth; a value of 2 corresponds to a PLL time constant of about 900 seconds and is recommended for room-temperature quartz oscillators. The time_maxerror and time_esterror variables track the maximum and estimated time errors in microseconds and grow automatically as the oscillator drifts between corrections. For PPS discipline, additional variables (pps_ybar, pps_disp) implement a frequency-lock loop with a median filter to handle jitter and signal loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The kernel keeps numbers for 'how far off is the time,' 'how fast the clock is running,' 'how tight should the feedback be,' and 'how much error is this worth?' These all have limits and scaling factors to avoid overflow and maintain precision.

sections.title: Status and Adoption
sections.content: RFC 1589 is an Informational RFC that does not specify a standard; rather, it documents an engineering model. The kernel model has been implemented in Unix kernels for Sun Microsystems (SunOS 4.1.x with SPARCstation hardware), Digital Equipment Corporation (Ultrix 4.x on DECstation 5000 and OSF/1 V1.x on AXP Alpha). For Digital equipment, the model provides microsecond-precision time-reading via interpolation between timer interrupts. The NTP Version 3 daemon (xntpd) automatically detects and uses these new system calls when they are available, providing synchronization accuracy limited only by the external source. A stand-alone simulator (kern.c) and reference implementation are available in the NTP distribution. The model remains relevant for any system requiring precise time synchronization and continues to inform modern kernel timekeeping designs.
sections.plainLanguage: This note describes how several real operating systems actually keep accurate clocks. It is not a standard everyone must follow, but many systems have used these ideas to improve their clocks and sync them to GPS.
